Plumber Resume Example & Writing Guide (2026)

A plumber resume has to prove one thing above all: that you can fix a problem right the first time, to code, and without a callback — and that a customer will ask for you by name next time. Hiring managers do not hire on a list of tools. They hire on licenses, code knowledge, and a record of jobs finished cleanly with happy customers.

This guide gives you a full annotated example, the skills hiring sides scan for, and the mistakes that cost interviews.

The example below is fictional, but every bullet follows the pattern that works.

Quick answer: A plumber resume should open with your license and trade experience, name the systems and sites you worked on, show code compliance and a clean safety record, list your certifications, and prove reliability on real jobs — then keep the layout single-column with standard headings so tracking systems parse every section cleanly.

Key Takeaways

  • Lead with your license and trade level — what you are licensed to do, and where.
  • Prove code and safety with inspections passed, callbacks avoided, and standards named.
  • Name the systems, sites, and scale from the posting.
  • Every bullet pairs a task with a result: what you fixed or installed, where, and what changed.
  • Keep the file single-column with standard headings and real text, so tracking systems parse it cleanly.

What Plumbing Hiring Managers Actually Look For

Talk to a master plumber or a service manager and you will not hear "passionate about pipes." You will hear:

  • License and trade level. Journeyman or master license, apprenticeship completed, and the states you are licensed in — checked before anything else.
  • Code and safety. Plumbing code knowledge, backflow prevention, gas line safety, and a clean safety record. "Zero failed inspections" is a hiring signal; "worked safely" is not.
  • Range across the trade. Service calls, new construction, remodels, and commercial work — water heaters, drain systems, gas lines, and fixtures. Name the systems and sites you actually worked on.
  • Jobs finished without callbacks. A repair that holds, a rough-in that passes inspection the first time.
  • Troubleshooting under pressure. Finding a hidden leak, clearing a main line, and fixing a problem without tearing a home apart — fast diagnosis is worth more than fast installation.

If your resume reads like a tool list — all wrenches and pipe, no jobs — it will lose to a work record.

Plumber Resume Example

Below is a complete example for a licensed journeyman plumber with residential service and new-construction experience. It is fictional — the name and figures are illustrative — but every bullet follows the pattern that works.

MARCUS BENNETT — Licensed Journeyman Plumber
Austin, TX · (512) 555-0147 · marcus.bennett@email.com · Licensed in TX

SUMMARY
Licensed journeyman plumber with 8 years of residential service and new-construction work. Led a 5-person crew repiping a 180-unit apartment complex; cut callbacks from 12% to 4% in one year and passed 35 consecutive inspections with zero failures. Water heaters, drain systems, gas lines, remodels; plumbing code current, OSHA 30, backflow certified.

LICENSES & CERTIFICATIONS
Texas Journeyman Plumber License · OSHA 30-Hour Construction · Backflow Prevention Assembly Tester · Medical Gas Certification · CPR / First Aid

SKILLS
Water heater installation & repair · Drain cleaning & camera inspection · Repiping & rough-in · Gas line installation & testing · Fixture installation & remodels · Sewer line repair & replacement · Backflow prevention · Blueprint & schematic reading · Leak detection & repair · Estimating & takeoffs · Crew leadership · Plumbing code compliance

PROFESSIONAL EXPERIENCE

Journeyman Plumber — Hill Country Plumbing, Austin, TX | 2021–Present - Led a 5-person crew repiping a 180-unit apartment complex, finishing rough-in 2 weeks ahead of schedule with zero failed inspections - Cut callbacks from 12% to 4% by introducing a pressure-test checklist and a same-day follow-up call routine, saving 100 crew-hours in one year - Replaced water heaters in 90 homes in a single season, with every job passing inspection on the first visit - Traced a recurring slab leak that two earlier callouts had missed, using camera inspection to find the break and repair it the same day - Train 3 apprentices; two of my apprentices passed their journeyman exams on the first attempt

Plumber — Austin Flow Plumbing, Austin, TX | 2018–2021 - Ran 25 service calls a week across the city, from drain clogs to full bathroom rough-ins, keeping every job inside its appointment window - Installed fixtures and supply lines across 10 restaurant fit-outs, including gas lines and grease interceptors to code - Read blueprints and marked up as-builts for the project manager, catching 6 pipe-routing clashes before they reached the site - Covered the lead plumber's holidays, running small commercial jobs end to end with no callbacks

Apprentice Plumber — Lone Star Plumbing, Austin, TX | 2016–2018 - Worked the rough-in crew on 80-unit residential builds, learning the pace of a real construction schedule from the inside - Set fixtures, ran supply lines, and cut pipe on commercial fit-outs, with a zero-missed-material record in the final year - Earned promotion to plumber after completing the apprenticeship and passing the journeyman exam

EDUCATION
Plumbing Apprenticeship — Associated Builders and Contractors, Austin, TX, 2016–2020 High School Diploma — Bowie High School, Austin, TX, 2016

Why it works: the summary leads with the two things plumbing hiring managers check first — license and jobs finished cleanly (180 units, callbacks 12% to 4%, 35 inspections passed) — then names the systems and certifications. Every bullet pairs a task with a result: faster rough-in, fewer callbacks.

Section-by-Section Breakdown

Summary: license, scope, safety record

"Licensed journeyman," "180-unit apartment complex," "callbacks from 12% to 4%," "35 inspections passed" — four facts that place you in thirty seconds. Lead with the license and a result, not training.

Experience: jobs with outcomes, not duties

Each bullet should answer "what changed because you fixed it?" "Installed plumbing in a commercial building" is a duty; "cut callbacks from 12% to 4% while holding the inspection schedule" is proof. Units repiped, inspections passed, callback rates, and crew size are the metrics that matter.

Systems and sites: proof you can work the trade

Your range is the closest thing to proof a plumber gets. Name the systems you actually installed — water heaters, drain systems, gas lines, fixtures — and the sites behind them. One vague claim costs more than a missing skill — only list work you could do tomorrow.

Skills: mirror the posting, honestly

List the systems and tools you have actually worked with, in the posting's own words — "camera inspection" versus "drain work" matters to filters, and so does "backflow prevention" versus "safety training." Depth in one part of the trade beats a long list.

Plumber Skills & ATS Keywords

Mirror the posting's language exactly — "camera inspection" vs "drain work" matters to filters:

  • Systems: water heater installation, drain cleaning, repiping, gas line installation, fixture installation, sewer line repair, backflow prevention
  • Work types: residential service calls, new-construction rough-in, remodels, restaurant fit-outs, commercial maintenance, emergency repair
  • Code & safety: plumbing code, backflow prevention, gas line safety, OSHA 30, inspection readiness, permit coordination
  • Tools & reading: blueprint reading, schematic reading, estimating & takeoffs, camera inspection, leak detection, crew leadership

Plumbing companies and facilities teams screen resumes through applicant tracking systems, and multi-column layouts and text-in-graphics are the usual parsing killers. 5 Mistakes That Cost Plumbers Interviews

  1. A tool list, not a work record. A long list of tools with no jobs, units, or inspections reads as a hobbyist. Add numbers that show you finished it.
  2. Hiding the license. If your license level and state are buried at the bottom, a hiring manager may never reach them. Put the license in the summary and header.
  3. Duties without results. "Installed plumbing in homes" could describe anyone on a crew. Add the result — fewer callbacks, faster rough-in, a crew trained — to every bullet.
  4. Vague system claims. List what you have actually installed, job after job.
  5. Ignoring code and safety. A resume with no mention of plumbing code, inspections, or safety training tells a hiring manager your work is a risk. Put your safety record up front.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do plumbers need a license to work?

Yes, in almost every state. Most plumbers work through an apprenticeship, then sit a journeyman exam for their state license. Some states also require a master license to pull permits or run a crew. Check your state's rules before you apply, and list every license you hold.

What experience should a new plumber put on a resume?

Lead with jobs and scope. An apprenticeship on a busy build, a repipe, or a water heater replacement all count. Name what you installed, how many units, and what changed — the same pattern as any senior bullet.

How do I show code compliance and safety on a plumber resume?

Name the record: inspections passed, callbacks avoided, and the standards you work to — plumbing code, backflow prevention, gas line safety. "35 inspections passed with zero failures" tells a manager more than any adjective.

Should a plumber resume include photos of my work?

No — keep the resume itself text-only so tracking systems can parse it, and put job photos in a separate portfolio or social profile linked from the header. A photo inside the resume file is usually stripped or misread by the parser.

How long should a plumber resume be?

One page for most plumbers, including experienced ones. Two pages only if you carry a long career across different work — service, new construction, and commercial — and even then keep your best numbers on page one.

Do I need to list every job I have ever held as a plumber?

No. List the jobs that show your trade range and your most recent work — usually the last 10 to 15 years, including your apprenticeship if it is your foundation. Older short roles can be dropped, but keep the timeline honest: a gap with no explanation raises more questions than a short role ever will.
